source_text: Δημιουργήματα δὲ ἐν αὐτῇ ὁ τῶν ὅλων κτίστης καὶ δημιουργὸς ἀπετέλεσε, φῶς νοητὸν πρέπον τῇ μακαριότητι τῶν φιλούντων τὸν Κύριον, τὰς λογικὰς καὶ ἀοράτους φύσεις, καὶ πᾶσαν τὴν τῶν νοητῶν διακόσμησιν, ὅσα τὴν ἡμετέραν διάνοιαν ὑπερβαίνει, ὧν οὐδὲ τὰς ὀνομασίας ἐξευρεῖν δυνατόν. Ταῦτα τοῦ ἀοράτου κόσμου συμπληροῖ τὴν οὐσίαν, ὡς διδάσκει ἡμᾶς ὁ Παῦλος, λέγων, Ὅτι ἐν αὐτῷ ἐκτίσθη τὰ πάντα, εἴτε ὁρατὰ, εἴτε ἀόρατα, εἴτε θρόνοι, εἴτε κυριότητες, εἴτε ἀρχαὶ, εἴτε ἐξουσίαι, εἴτε δυνάμεις, εἴτε ἀγγέλων στρατιαὶ, εἴτε ἀρχαγγέλων ἐπιστασίαι· ὅτε δὲ ἔδει λοιπὸν καὶ τὸν κόσμον τοῦτον ἐπεισαχθῆναι τοῖς οὖσι, προηγουμένως μὲν διδασκαλεῖον καὶ παιδευτήριον τῶν ἀνθρωπίνων ψυχῶν· ἔπειτα μέντοι καὶ ἁπαξαπλῶς πάντων τῶν ἐν γενέσει καὶ φθορᾷ ἐπιτήδειον ἐνδιαίτημα. Συμφυὴς ἄρα τῷ κόσμῳ, καὶ τοῖς ἐν αὐτῷ ζῴοις τε καὶ φυτοῖς, ἡ τοῦ χρόνου διέξοδος ὑπέστη, ἐπειγομένη ἀεὶ καὶ παραρρέουσα, καὶ μηδαμοῦ παυομένη τοῦ δρόμου. Ἢ οὐχὶ τοιοῦτος ὁ χρόνος, οὗ τὸ μὲν παρελθὸν ἠφανίσθη, τὸ δὲ μέλλον οὔπω πάρεστι, τὸ δὲ παρὸν πρὶν γνωσθῆναι διαδιδράσκει τὴν αἴσθησιν; Τοιαύτη δέ τις καὶ τῶν γινομένων ἡ φύσις, ἢ αὐξανομένη πάντως, ἢ φθίνουσα, τὸ δὲ ἱδρυμένον καὶ στάσιμον οὐκ ἐπίδηλον ἔχουσα. Ἔπρεπεν οὖν τοῖς ζῴων τε καὶ φυτῶν σώμασιν, οἱονεὶ ῥεύματί τινι πρὸς ἀνάγκην ἐνδεδεμένοις, καὶ τῇ πρὸς γένεσιν ἢ φθορὰν ἀγούσῃ κινήσει συνεχομένοις, ὑπὸ τῆς τοῦ χρόνου φύσεως περιέχεσθαι, συγγενῆ τοῖς ἀλλοιουμένοις κεκτημένου τὴν ἰδιότητα. Ἐντεῦθεν οἰκείως ἐπέβαλε τῷ περὶ αὐτὸν λόγῳ ὁ σοφῶς ἡμᾶς τοῦ κόσμου τὴν γένεσιν ἐκδιδάσκων, εἰπὼν, Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἐποίησεν· τουτέστιν, ἐν ἀρχῇ ταύτῃ τῇ κατὰ χρόνον. Οὐ γὰρ δὴ κατὰ πρεσβυγένειαν πάντων τῶν γενομένων προέχειν αὐτὸν μαρτυρῶν λέγει ἐν ἀρχῇ γεγονέναι, ἀλλὰ μετὰ τὰ ἀόρατα καὶ νοούμενα τῶν ὁρατῶν τούτων καὶ αἰσθήσει ληπτῶν τὴν ἀρχὴν τῆς ὑπάρξεως διηγεῖται. Λέγεται μὲν οὖν ἀρχὴ καὶ ἡ πρώτη κίνησις· ὡς, Ἀρχὴ ὁδοῦ ἀγαθῆς τὸ ποιεῖν δίκαια. Ἀπὸ γὰρ τῶν δικαίων πράξεων πρῶτον κινούμεθα πρὸς τὸν μακάριον βίον. Λέγεται δὲ ἀρχὴ καὶ ὅθεν γίνεταί τι, τοῦ ἐνυπάρχοντος αὐτῷ ὡς ἐπὶ οἰκίας θεμέλιος, καὶ ἐπὶ πλοίου ἡ τρόπις, καθὸ εἴρηται, Ἀρχὴ σοφίας, φόβος Κυρίου. Οἷον γὰρ κρηπὶς καὶ βάθρον πρὸς τὴν τελείωσιν ἡ εὐλά βεια. Ἀρχὴ δὲ καὶ τῶν τεχνικῶν ἔργων ἡ τέχνη· ὡς ἡ σοφία Βεσελεὴλ, τοῦ περὶ τὴν σκηνὴν κόσμου. Ἀρχὴ δὲ πράξεων πολλάκις καὶ τὸ εὔχρηστον τέλος τῶν γινομένων· ὡς τῆς ἐλεημοσύνης ἡ παρὰ Θεοῦ ἀποδοχὴ, καὶ πάσης τῆς κατ' ἀρετὴν ἐνεργείας τὸ ἐν ἐπαγγελίαις ἀποκείμενον τέλος. 1.6 Τοσαυταχῶς οὖν λεγομένης τῆς ἀρχῆς, σκόπει εἰ μὴ πᾶσι τοῖς σημαινομένοις ἡ παροῦσα φωνὴ ἐφαρμόσει. Καὶ γὰρ ἀφ' οὗ χρόνου ἤρξατο ἡ τοῦ κόσμου τούτου σύστασις, δυνατόν σοι μαθεῖν, ἐάν γε ἐκ τοῦ παρόντος εἰς τὸ κατόπιν ἀναποδίζων, φιλονεικήσῃς εὑρεῖν τὴν πρώτην ἡμέραν τῆς τοῦ κόσμου γενέσεως. Εὑρήσεις γὰρ οὕτως, πόθεν τῷ χρόνῳ ἡ πρώτη κίνησις, ἔπειτα, ὅτι καὶ οἱονεὶ θεμέλιοί τινες καὶ κρηπῖδες προκατεβλήθησαν ὁ οὐρανὸς καὶ ἡ γῆ· εἶτα, ὅτι ἐστί τις τεχνικὸς λόγος ὁ καθηγησάμενος τῆς τῶν ὁρωμένων διακοσμήσεως, ὡς ἐνδείκνυταί σοι ἡ φωνὴ τῆς ἀρχῆς· καὶ τὸ μὴ εἰκῇ μηδὲ μάτην, ἀλλὰ πρός τι τέλος ὠφέλιμον καὶ μεγάλην χρείαν τοῖς οὖσι συνεισφερόμενον ἐπινενοῆσθαι τὸν κόσμον, εἴπερ τῷ ὄντι ψυχῶν λογικῶν διδασκαλεῖον καὶ θεογνωσίας ἐστὶ παιδευτήριον, διὰ τῶν ὁρωμένων καὶ αἰσθητῶν χειραγωγίαν τῷ νῷ παρεχόμενος πρὸς τὴν θεωρίαν τῶν ἀοράτων, καθά φησιν ὁ ἀπόστολος, ὅτι Τὰ ἀόρατα αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ κτίσεως κόσμου τοῖς ποιήμασι νοούμενα καθορᾶται.
thought_title: The invisible creation and the meanings of 'beginning'
orientation: Basil is explaining what existed before the visible world and why Genesis says 'In the beginning God made,' distinguishing the invisible creation from the temporal beginning of the visible world.
pass_a_gloss: And in it the Creator and Maker of all things completed his works: a light intelligible, befitting the blessedness of those who love the Lord, the rational and invisible natures, and all the ordering of the intelligible things, as many as surpass our understanding, of which not even the names it is possible to find out. These things complete the substance of the invisible world, as Paul teaches us, saying, 'Because in him were created all things, whether visible, whether invisible, whether thrones, whether dominions, whether principalities, whether authorities, whether powers, whether armies of angels, whether ranks of archangels.' But when it was necessary henceforth that this world also be introduced among existing things, first of all as a school and training place of human souls; then indeed also simply as a suitable dwelling for all things that are in generation and corruption. A connatural then with the world, and with the animals and plants in it, the passage of time came into being, always hurrying and flowing past, and nowhere stopping in its course. Or is not time such a thing, of which the past has vanished, the future is not yet present, and the present slips away from perception before it is known? And such also is the nature of things that come to be, either always growing, or wasting away, and not having the fixed and stable clearly evident. It was fitting therefore that the bodies of animals and plants, as if bound by necessity to some stream, and held together by the movement that leads to generation or corruption, should be encompassed by the nature of time, which possesses a property akin to things that are altered. Hence fittingly he applied to the account concerning it the one who wisely teaches us the origin of the world, saying, 'In the beginning he made'; that is, in this beginning, the one according to time. For he does not say that it came to be in the beginning, testifying that it excels all things that have come to be in seniority, but after the invisible and intelligible things he narrates the beginning of the existence of these visible things and things perceptible by sense. Beginning then is also called the first movement; as, 'The beginning of a good way is to do righteous things.' For from righteous actions we are first moved toward the blessed life. And beginning is also called that from which something comes to be, of what exists in it, as in a house the foundation, and in a ship the keel, according to which it is said, 'The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord.' For like a base and a step toward perfection is piety. And beginning of artistic works is the art; as the wisdom of Bezalel, of the adornment concerning the tabernacle. And beginning of actions often is also the useful end of the things that come to be; as of almsgiving the acceptance by God, and of every activity according to virtue the end stored up in promises. 1.6 Since beginning then is said in so many ways, consider whether the present word will not fit all the meanings. For from what time the constitution of this world began, it is possible for you to learn, if indeed from the present going back to what is behind, you strive to find the first day of the world's origin. For you will find thus, whence for time the first movement, then, that also as it were certain foundations and bases were laid down beforehand, the heaven and the earth; then, that there is some artistic reason that guided the ordering of the visible things, as the word 'beginning' indicates to you; and that not at random nor in vain, but toward some useful end and great need for existing things the world was thought out, if indeed in truth it is a school of rational souls and a training place of the knowledge of God, through the visible and perceptible things providing guidance by the hand to the mind toward the contemplation of the invisible things, as the apostle says, that 'His invisible things from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things made.'

choices.why: Keeps the adjective postposed as in Greek, emphasizing the kind of light (perceivable by mind, not senses) rather than a fixed compound
Literal rendering of both adjectives with the noun, preserving the pair as Basil's description of angelic beings
Renders the adverb's sense of primary purpose, matching the μὲν...ἔπειτα μέντοι contrast
Keeps the philosophical pair as a fixed phrase for the realm of coming-to-be and passing-away

choices.why: Preserves the 'as if' (οἱονεὶ) and the dative of binding (ἐνδεδεμένοις) with the stream image

choices.english: providing guidance by the hand to the mind
choices.why: Renders χειραγωγία literally as 'guidance by the hand,' keeping the metaphor of leading a child by the hand toward knowledge

pass_b_english: In that world the Creator and Maker of all things brought his works to completion: an intelligible light suited to the blessedness of those who love the Lord, the rational and invisible natures, and the whole ordering of the intelligible realm, all that surpasses our understanding, whose very names we cannot discover. These things fill up the substance of the invisible world, as Paul teaches us when he says, “For in him all things were created, whether visible or invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities or powers, whether angelic hosts or archangelic ministries” (Colossians 1:16). But when it was time for this world also to be introduced among the things that exist, it was first of all a school and training place of human souls, and then also a dwelling place suited to all things in generation and corruption. The course of time, then, came into being as something natural to the world and to the animals and plants within it, always pressing forward and flowing past, never pausing in its race. Is time not exactly this: the past has vanished, the future is not yet here, and the present slips away from our perception before it can be known? The nature of things that come to be is like this too: always either growing or wasting away, with no evident fixedness or stability. It was fitting, therefore, that the bodies of animals and plants, bound as if by necessity to some stream and held fast by the movement that leads them toward generation or corruption, should be contained by the nature of time, which possesses a property akin to the things that change. For this reason the one who wisely teaches us the origin of the world fittingly began his account of it by saying, “In the beginning God made”—that is, in this beginning according to time. For he does not say it came to be in the beginning, testifying that it precedes all created things in age; rather, after the invisible and intelligible realities, he recounts the beginning of the existence of these visible things that are grasped by the senses. “Beginning” is also used of first movement, as in, “The beginning of a good way is to do what is right” (Proverbs 16:5 LXX). For it is from righteous actions that we are first moved toward the blessed life. “Beginning” is also used of that from which something comes, as the foundation is in a house and the keel in a ship, according to what is said: “The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord” (Proverbs 1:7; cf. Psalm 111:10 LXX). For reverence is like a base and a pedestal for perfection. The beginning of works of craft is the craft itself, as the wisdom of Bezalel was the beginning of the adornment of the tabernacle. And the beginning of actions is often the useful end of what comes to be, as the acceptance from God is the beginning of almsgiving, and the end stored up in the promises is the beginning of every activity according to virtue. Since “beginning” is used in so many ways, consider whether the present word does not fit all its meanings. You can learn from what time the constitution of this world began, if you go back from the present into the past and earnestly seek to find the first day of the world's origin. For in this way you will discover whence time received its first movement, and then that heaven and earth were laid down beforehand like foundations and bases, and then that there is some craftsmanlike reason that guided the ordering of the visible things, as the word “beginning” indicates to you. And you will discover that the world was not devised at random or in vain, but for some useful end and to contribute great benefit to the things that exist, if indeed it is truly a school for rational souls and a training place for the knowledge of God, providing guidance by the hand to the mind through visible and perceptible things toward the contemplation of the invisible, as the apostle says: “His invisible attributes, understood through the things that have been made since the creation of the world, are clearly seen” (Romans 1:20).

problems.source_quote: Ἀρχὴ ὁδοῦ ἀγαθῆς τὸ ποιεῖν δίκαια
problems.why: This is Proverbs 16:11 in LXX numbering, not Psalm 110:10. Psalm 110 (Hebrew 111) has no verse 10; it has 10 verses total. The verse "The beginning of a good way is to do what is right" does not appear in Psalms at all.
problems.ruling: Ἀρχὴ ὁδοῦ ἀγαθῆς τὸ ποιεῖν δίκαια is Proverbs, not Psalm 110:10; wrong scripture reference misleads reader.

problems.why: The verse "The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord" is Psalm 110:10 LXX / Hebrew 111:10 only in some numbering confusion, but actually this is Psalm 111:10 (Hebrew 112:10) in standard LXX, or Proverbs 1:7. However, Basil attributes it with "καθὸ εἴρηται" and the English triple citation is garbled. The verse is Proverbs 1:7 primarily, and Psalm 110:10 does not exist. The English invents a non-existent Psalm 110:10.
problems.ruling: Ἀρχὴ σοφίας φόβος Κυρίου is Psalm 110:10 LXX; triple citation is garbled and misleading.
